L29: We propose and evaluate an empirical method for water depth determination from hyperspectral imagery when the benthic layer is visible using support vector regression (SVR). The implementation of the empirical method is presented, and its ability to estimate water depths is compared with a more commonly used band ratio method for two distinct fluvial environments.
L30: Our analysis shows that SVR outperforms the band ratio method by providing better root-mean-square error (RMSE) agreement and higher $R^2$ for both clear and turbid water. We also demonstrate an extension of the nonparametric properties of SVR to provide estimates of water turbidity from hyperspectral imagery and show that the approach is able to estimate turbidity with an RMSE of approximately 1.2 NTU when compared with independent turbidity measurements.

L106: I. I NTRODUCTION
L107: 
L108: B ATHYMETRY estimates provide the research commu-
L109: 
L110: nity with quantitative spatially distributed models that
L111: 
L112: allow the development of hydraulic and mesohabitat models
L113: 
L114: [1]. Acquiring bathymetry through remote sensing techniques
L115: is well established and has been applied successfully in both
L116: 
L117: coastal and inland ﬂuvial environments [2]. Remote sens-
L118: 
L119: ing can yield accurate quantitative bathymetry using typical
L120: 
L121: methods such as echosounders, airborne bathymetric LiDAR
L122: 
L123: and passive optical imagery [3]. Due to their relatively high
L124: 
L125: spatial resolution and accuracy, improved spectral resolu-
L126: 
L127: tion, and easily implemented image processing techniques,
L128: 
L129: multi/hyperspectral imagery has emerged as a popular method
L130: for bathymetry retrieval [4].
L131: 
L132: Bathymetry using passive multispectral imagery can provide
L133: 
L134: relatively high accuracy and source imagery can be easily
L135: 
L136: accessed through a number of free or low cost portals. Once
L137: 
L138: acquired, the algorithms to process the imagery are available in
L139: 
L140: many conventional image processing software packages. The

L169: 
L170: physical principle behind passive optical image bathymetry is
L171: 
L172: that water depth, substrate type, water column properties and
L173: water surface roughness all affect the observed reﬂectance [5].
L174: 
L175: Water attenuates the propagated light due to scattering and ab-
L176: 
L177: sorption in water body, with a rate of attenuation depending on
L178: 
L179: wavelength. Through investigation of water optical properties,
L180: 
L181: many analytical and empirical methods have been proposed to
L182: 
L183: retrieve water depth directly from passive multi/hyperspectral
L184: 
L185: imagery. Lyzenga [6] and Philpot [7] proposed and validated
L186: 
L187: the efﬁcacy of passive remote sensing for water bathymetry
L188: retrieval using a linear solution. Legleiter et al. [5] proposed a
L189: 
L190: band ratio method to retrieve bathymetry from passive optical
L191: 
L192: imagery data using a statistical test to select an optimal band
L193: 
L194: pair for bathymetric regression. Bachmann et al. [8] used
L195: 
L196: a manifold coordinate representation to retrieve bathymetry
L197: 
L198: from hyperspectral imagery with a reduced representation.
L199: 
L200: Sandidge et al. [9] used the Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging
L201: 
L202: Spectrometer (AVIRIS) data to train a neural network system
L203: to retrieve bathymetry with established quantitative empirical
L204: 
L205: relationship.
L206: 
L207: The band ratio method implemented by Legleiter et al. [5]
L208: 
L209: and Ma et al. [10] has been shown in the literature to be
L210: 
L211: easy to implement, provide accurate bathymetric results from
L212: 
L213: hyperspectral imagery, and have a minimum number of tuning
L214: 
L215: parameters. The main drawback of the band ratio method is
L216: 
L217: that only a portion of the spectral information is utilized;
L218: 
L219: however, all bands theoretically are attenuated by the water
L220: column with speciﬁc but wavelength dependent attenuation
L221: 
L222: coefﬁcients. Therefore all spectral bands should potentially
L223: 
L224: contain water bathymetry information. A more generalized
L225: 
L226: model, which takes advantage of a number of spectral channels
L227: 
L228: could potentially improve bathymetric estimates. However,
L229: 
L230: a speciﬁc model would be difﬁcult to contruct due to the
L231: 
L232: complex and unknown relationship between the spectral bands
L233: 
L234: and the water column response. A non-parametric method
L235: which utilizes all spectral information can be formulated, and
L236: 
L237: could potentially improve bathymetry retrieval. It would also
L238: 
L239: be preferable, if like the OBRA method the algorithm could
L240: 
L241: be easily implemented without a requirement for extensive
L242: 
L243: radiative transfer modeling.
L244: 
L245: Support vector machine (SVM) is a supervised machine
L246: 
L247: learning algorithm used to analyze patterns within data, and
L248: 
L249: support vector regression (SVR) is a realization of support
L250: vector machine for prediction [11]. SVR is a non-parametric
L251: 
L252: regression method but also a data dependent learning scheme
L253: 
L254: and thus no explicit model is required to fuse the observations
L255: 
L256: IEEE GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING LETTERS 2
L257: 
L258: with the physical measurement quantities. The regression
L259: 
L260: model is generalized, and can be used to estimate any spec-
L261: 
L262: trally related parameters where no explicit physical model
L263: 
L264: exists. A review of support vector machines and regression
L265: can be found in [12]. Bruzzone et al. [13] have estimated
L266: 
L267: biophysical parameters from remotely sensed data using a
L268: 
L269: multiple estimator system which incorporated SVM in com-
L270: 
L271: bination with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network.
L272: 
L273: Camps-Valls et al. [14] utilized the SVR method to estimate
L274: 
L275: ocean chlorophyll concentration with satellite remote sensing
L276: 
L277: data to provide a more accurate, less biased, and noise resistant
L278: 
L279: model.
L280: 
L281: In this letter, we propose and test using SVR as an al-
L282: ternative method for bathymetric retrieval in order to more
L283: 
L284: accurately account for the nonlinearity existing in the observed
L285: 
L286: hyperspectral data. A conventional band ratio bathymetry
L287: 
L288: retrieval method is used as a baseline for comparison with the
L289: 
L290: proposed SVR method, and a comparison with in-situ water
L291: 
L292: depth observations is presented. To demonstrate the generality
L293: 
L294: of the SVR method, we also evaluate its ability to predict other
L295: 
L296: water column parameters empirically by using it to estimate
L297: water turbidity from hyperspectral imagery. We again compare
L298: 
L299: the results to in-situ measurements of turbidity.

L35: A multispectral full-waveform light detection and ranging (LiDAR) instrument prototype with four wavelengths and a supercontinuum laser as a light source was designed to monitor the fine structure and the biochemical parameters of vegetation. Components of the instrument included a 2-D scanning platform, a supercontinuum laser source, a receiving optical system, and a multichannel full-waveform measurement module.
L36: The LiDAR instrument can simultaneously measure multichannel-returned full-waveform laser signals. Position information in the recorded waveform allowed us to compute the distance from the target, whereas the intensity of the signal provided the spectral reflectance. Performance for the measuring distance and the spectrum was evaluated.
L37: Experiments indicated that the instrument has high measurement accuracy and has the ability to detect the biochemical characteristics of vegetation via construction of the normalized difference vegetation index and the photochemical reflectance index. The experiment also indicated that the instrument has the potential to generate spectral 3-D point clouds.
L38: Therefore, the instrument could play a significant role in detecting the vertical distribution of structural and biochemical characteristics of vegetation.

L185: 
L186: Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) has the advantage of a
L187: 
L188: high spatial resolution, an anti-interference ability, and a high
L189: 
L190: detection sensitivity. As an active remote sensing technology,
L191: 
L192: LiDAR is minimally inﬂuenced by illumination condition or
L193: 
L194: shadows. Terrestrial or airborne LiDAR instruments mainly
L195: 
L196: use monochrome lasers to recode the intensity of received
L197: signals, as well as to provide accurate geometric information.
L198: 
L199: Traditional single-wavelength LiDAR has been widely used in
L200: 
L201: the estimations of individual tree height, biomass at the plot
L202: 
L203: level, and forest vertical structures [2]. Of late, radiometric cali-
L204: 
L205: bration techniques have signiﬁcantly promoted the applications
L206: 
L207: of intensity information [3], [4]. However, intensity information
L208: 
L209: obtained for a target is inﬂuenced by many factors, including
L210: the laser’s power, the transmitting distance, the incidence angle,
L211: 
L212: the reﬂectivity of the target, and the absorption of the medium.
L213: 
L214: Therefore, it is difﬁcult to obtain biochemical components
L215: 
L216: from single-wavelength LiDAR observations. Other studies
L217: 
L218: have indicated that a combination of spectral information and
L219: 
L220: LiDAR information can improve accuracy for extracting these
L221: 
L222: parameters [5], [6].
L223: 
L224: A full-waveform LiDAR can record the entire returned laser
L225: pulse at a reliable sampling rate, even as an emitted laser pulse
L226: 
L227: penetrates the vegetation canopy. Therefore, a waveform proﬁle
L228: 
L229: through the depth of the canopy can be generated. Vertical
L230: 
L231: structure measurements of the forest canopy can be obtained
L232: 
L233: using a waveform analysis [7]. Radiative transfer model and
L234: 
L235: geometrical optic model simulations indicate that the changes
L236: 
L237: in forest leaf area density, leaf angle, and biochemical com-
L238: 
L239: position can be explained using variations of the waveform
L240: 
L241: [8], [9].
L242: Currently, passive optical sensors are able to perform multi-
L243: 
L244: spectral acquisitions, whereas active commercial LiDAR sen-
L245: 
L246: sors perform measurements in a single wavelength. Both the

L313: The multispectral waveform LiDAR system proposed in this
L314: 
L315: letter is composed of the following subsystems (see Fig. 1):

L318: 
L319: source; 3) a coaxial optical transmitting and receiving system

L322: 
L323: data acquisition system; and 5) a control center. The pulsed

L326: 450–2400 nm produces a ∼1- to 2-ns pulse at a repetition rate

L328: of 24 kHz. Broadband light emitted by the laser is collimated

L330: (the divergence angle is less than 5 mrad) when passing through

L332: the refracting collimator. The collimated beam is reﬂected twice

L335: 
L336: axis of the telescope. The mirror M1 is also used as a beam

L338: sampler plate for transmitting a small portion of emitted light

L340: 
L341: detection sensor. The APD1 sensor is used to collect a sample
